title: Run, Ravi, Run!
paragraphs:
The field is marked with bright white lanes,
as straight as the lines in a new exercise book.
Ravi crouches at the start,
his tummy full of butterflies,
his legs as wobbly as jelly.
The whistle shrieks. The crowd begins to chant:
Run, Ravi, run!

He shoots off the line like an arrow.
The wind roars in his ears,
the finishing tape flutters far ahead,
and for ten long strides
he is in front of everyone.
Run, Ravi, run!

Then his shoelace catches.
The world tips sideways
and the ground rushes up to meet him:
grass in his mouth, a sting in his knee.
The others thunder past
in a blur of red and blue.
The chanting stops.

Ravi could stay there.
He could limp to the side
and pretend he doesn’t care.
But then, from the crowd, one small voice:
his little sister Priya, high on Dad’s shoulders,
shouting as loudly as she can,
Run, Ravi, run!

So he gets up.
He runs with a grazed knee and a flapping lace,
long after the winner has crossed the line,
and one by one, the crowd joins in
until the whole field roars:
Run, Ravi, run!

He finishes last.
No medal, no ribbon, no sticker,
just the loudest cheer of the whole day
and Priya’s arms around his neck.
Well run, Ravi.
Well run.

questions.prompt:
Look at verse 1.
How does the poet show that Ravi is nervous before the race?
Give **two** examples from the poem.
questions.model: The poet says that Ravi has ‘his tummy full of butterflies’, which means he feels fluttery and sick with nerves. His legs are also ‘as wobbly as jelly’, which shows that they are shaking.
points: each different example from verse 1 (1 mark each), such as:
‘his tummy full of butterflies’: he feels fluttery or sick with nerves
‘his legs as wobbly as jelly’: his legs are shaking

questions.prompt:
Look at verse 1.
Find and copy **one** word that shows the whistle makes a sudden, loud, high sound.

Look at verse 3.
What makes Ravi fall? Tick **one**.
options: Another runner pushes him.
His shoelace catches.
He slips on wet grass.
He trips over the finishing tape.

questions.prompt:
Look at verse 3.
‘The world tips sideways
and the ground rushes up to meet him’
What do these lines tell you about Ravi’s fall?
questions.model: They show that the fall happens suddenly and fast: Ravi loses his balance, everything seems to tilt, and he hits the ground before he knows what is happening.
points: explaining that the fall is sudden or fast, or that Ravi loses his balance and everything seems to tilt as he hits the ground.

questions.prompt:
Look at verse 3.
Why does the chanting stop? Tick **one**.
options: The race has finished.
The crowd has lost their voices.
The crowd is shocked and worried because Ravi has fallen.
Ravi has won the race.

questions.prompt:
Look at verse 4.
‘He could limp to the side’
Which word is closest in meaning to **limp**? Tick **one**.
options: sprint
hobble
skip
march

questions.prompt:
Look at verse 4.
After Ravi falls, who is the first person in the crowd to shout to him?

Look at the whole poem.
Tick **one** box in each row to show whether each statement is **true** or **false**.
statements: The lanes on the field are white.
Ravi is in front of everyone for the whole race.
The other runners pass Ravi in a blur of red and blue.

questions.prompt:
Look at the whole poem.
Why does the poet keep repeating ‘Run, Ravi, run!’? Tick **one**.
options: to show that Ravi is running away from the crowd
to show that people keep cheering Ravi on
to show that the race is very short
to show that Ravi keeps falling over

questions.prompt:
Look at verse 6.
Why does the poem end with ‘Well run, Ravi.’ instead of ‘Run, Ravi, run!’? Tick **one**.
options: because Ravi has to run the race again
because the crowd is cross that Ravi came last
because the race is over, and Ravi is being praised for how he ran
because Ravi has won the race

questions.prompt:
Look at verses 5 and 6.
Ravi finishes last, but he gets ‘the loudest cheer of the whole day’. Why?
Explain, using evidence from the poem.
questions.model: Ravi gets the loudest cheer because he does not give up. He falls and hurts his knee, but ‘he gets up’ and keeps running, even ‘long after the winner has crossed the line’. The crowd admire how brave and determined he is, so ‘one by one, the crowd joins in’ to cheer him all the way to the finish.
points: Explains that Ravi fell but did not give up and finished the race, with evidence, such as ‘So he gets up.’ or ‘long after the winner has crossed the line’.
Explains that the crowd admired his courage or determination, with evidence, such as ‘one by one, the crowd joins in’.

questions.prompt:
What do you think Ravi will do at next year’s sports day?
Use evidence from the poem to support your prediction.
questions.model: I think Ravi will run in the race again and try his hardest, because he did not give up this year: ‘So he gets up.’ He will probably tie his laces tightly first, because this year ‘his shoelace catches’ and made him fall. Remembering ‘the loudest cheer of the whole day’ will help him to feel brave.
points: a sensible prediction (1 mark), e.g. he will run again and not give up; he will tie his laces tightly; he will be less nervous.

evidence from the poem that supports the prediction (1 mark), e.g. he got up and finished the race; his shoelace caught and made him fall; he got ‘the loudest cheer of the whole day’; Priya cheered for him.

questions.prompt: Which is the best summary of the whole poem? Tick **one**.
options: Ravi practises hard and wins his sports day race.
Ravi hurts his knee and has to stop running for the rest of the day.
Ravi watches the race from the crowd and cheers for the winner.
Ravi falls over in a race, but he gets up and finishes, and the crowd cheers him loudly.
